title: upekkha
hookLine: upekkha; the steady mind in a storm
carry: let it be as it is
tomorrow: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
last: THE JATAKA — THE BRIDGE HE MADE OF HIS BODY.

cards: Monday, the boss calls the work brilliant, and the whole day floats. Tuesday, a client calls it the worst thing they've seen, and sleep won't come. Wednesday, a friend forgets a birthday.
Thursday, a stranger compliments a coat, and suddenly it's fine again. Up, down, up, down, like a boat in weather. Plenty of weeks go like that, and it gets called being human.
It is. But the Buddha named those winds, one by one, and taught a way to stand in them without being blown over. Today, the steady mind in a storm.

teach.b: Upekkha. Equanimity. It's the fourth of the divine abodes you met with karuna: friendliness, compassion, gladness, and this.
The word comes from a root meaning to look, with a prefix meaning over or near. To look on, from a steady place. Not to look away.
The Buddha named eight worldly conditions, four pairs, often pictured as winds. Gain and loss. Fame and disgrace.
Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. The text says they come to everyone, the untaught and the wise alike.
The winds aren't the problem. Getting flung around by them is.
The Dhammapada has the picture: "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." A rock. The wind still blows.
The rock still feels it. It just doesn't move. Here's the part of upekkha that's easy to get wrong.
Equanimity isn't indifference. Buddhaghosa warned of its near enemy, a dull, unknowing calm that looks like it but isn't. Some teachers today call that indifference.
Indifference says, I don't care. Equanimity says, I care, and I'm not going to be knocked over. It comes last of the four, and here's one way to see why.

teach.h: LET IT BE AS IT IS.
teach.b: Metta wishes well. Karuna stays with pain. Mudita is glad for others.
And upekkha keeps all of that steady, so the caring doesn't burn you out. A good nurse, a good parent, a good friend in an emergency. Warm, and calm.

how: Buddhists cultivate upekkha as one of the four brahmaviharas, often after metta, karuna and mudita, by reflecting that beings meet the results of their own actions, and by practicing steadiness through life's gains and losses.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: one pair of the eight winds

s: indifference is its near enemy. equanimity cares, and isn't knocked over.
the Buddha named eight worldly conditions
gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain.
upekkha is the fourth of the divine abodes

games.q: you get a glowing review at work, then harsh criticism the next day. according to the teaching on the eight winds, what's the goal?
o: feel both, and stay steady like a rock.
games.why: the winds still blow, and the rock still feels them. it just isn't moved. equanimity isn't escaping the winds; it's standing in them.

practice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit tall and steady, like a rock on a hillside. Now let one wind blow: remember a moment of praise.
Notice what it does in your body. Let it pass. Now let the other blow: a moment of blame.
Notice that too. Let it pass. Come back to the breath, and to the weight of your body on the seat.
The winds come and go. You stay.

wordCard.voice: Equanimity. Upekkha: looking on from a steady place, a rock in the eight winds. Caring, and not knocked over. Nineteenth word.

orig.note: Pali: equanimity, looking on. Sanskrit: upekṣā. The fourth brahmavihāra.

carryVoice: Your line: let it be as it is. Letting things be as they are, and still showing up. Day nineteen, done.

sources.q: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
